content: 1. In patients requiring peripheral intravenous catheters (PIVCs), peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs), or peripheral arterial catheters (PACs) across all age groups (adults, adolescents, children, and neonates), the use of a defined sterile or aseptic protocol for catheter access is compared to the absence of such a protocol. The impact on bloodstream infection rates associated with PIVC-associated infections (BSI-PIVCAIC) and mortality is evaluated. 2. In patients requiring PIVCs or PICCs across all age groups, the use of a closed-access device system (e.g., luer lock) is compared to an open-access device system. The outcomes assessed include the rates of BSI-PIVCAIC and mortality. 3. In patients with PICCs across all age groups, the use of single-lumen PICCs is compared to multi-lumen PICCs. The impact on BSI-PIVCAIC rates and mortality is analyzed. 4. In patients requiring PIVCs or PICCs across all age groups, catheter removal based on predefined schedules is compared to removal only when clinically indicated due to suspected or confirmed complications. The outcomes of interest include BSI-PIVCAIC rates and mortality. 5. The timing of scheduled catheter removal (e.g., 72–96 hours post-insertion) or activity-based removal (e.g., 2 days post-surgery) is assessed to determine whether the impact on BSI-PIVCAIC rates and mortality varies. 6. In patients requiring PIVCs or PICCs across all age groups, the removal or replacement of catheters within 24 hours when inserted under emergency conditions is compared to not removing or replacing them within 24 hours. The outcomes assessed include BSI-PIVCAIC rates and mortality. 7. In patients requiring intravenous (IV) access for antibiotic or chemotherapy administration across all age groups, the use of PICCs is compared to PIVCs. The outcomes evaluated include BSI-PIVCAIC rates, mortality, complications related to IV catheter insertion, infusion-related complications (e.g., occlusions), and catheter dwell time. 8. In patients requiring IV access for antibiotic or chemotherapy administration across all age groups, the use of PICCs is compared to midline vascular catheters (MVCs). The outcomes assessed include BSI-PIVCAIC rates, mortality, the number of IV insertion attempts, insertion-related complications, infusion-related complications (e.g., occlusions), and catheter dwell time. 9. The systematic review adhered to Cochrane methodology and the Framework for Rating Evidence in Public Health. Reporting followed the PRISMA checklist, and studies published from 1980 onwards, regardless of language, country, or setting, were included. 10. Comparisons included sterile techniques versus non-sterile techniques, chlorhexidine-containing antiseptics versus non-chlorhexidine antiseptics, ultrasound-guided insertion versus non-ultrasound-guided insertion, and other factors such as catheter material (silicon vs. polyurethane), dressing type (occlusive vs. non-occlusive), and clinician training. 11. Maintenance protocols, such as formal sterile dressing versus no formal protocol, continuous infusion versus intermittent infusion, and systematic sterile flushing versus no flushing, were also evaluated for their impact on outcomes. 12. Removal strategies, including scheduled removal versus clinically indicated removal and removal within 24 hours under emergency conditions, were assessed for their effects on BSI-PIVCAIC rates and mortality. 13. The outcomes of interest included catheter-associated bloodstream infections, local infections, BSI-related mortality, all-cause mortality, sepsis, phlebitis, thrombophlebitis, edema, hematoma, fluid or blood leakage, infiltration, accidental removal, obstruction, and catheter longevity. 14. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) rated the importance of outcomes using a modified Delphi approach. Outcomes rated as critical for decision-making included BSI, BSI-related mortality, and sepsis, among others. 15. Studies assessing multimodal or bundled interventions were included in the review process but not synthesized in the evidence due to challenges in identifying causal pathways. 16. A systematic literature search was conducted in multiple databases, covering studies from January 1980 to March 2023. Manual searches of reference lists and consultation with topic experts were also performed. 17. Study selection involved dual independent review of titles and abstracts, with conflicts resolved by consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. Reasons for exclusion were documented, and authors were contacted for clarification when necessary. 18. Data extraction was performed using a structured form, with a second reviewer verifying completeness and accuracy. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus or involvement of a senior reviewer. 19. The extracted data included study design, eligibility criteria, interventions, population characteristics, sample size, attrition, and outcomes of interest. Intention-to-treat results were recorded when available. 20. Risk of bias was assessed using established tools, such as the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for randomized controlled trials and the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized studies. Outcomes were categorized as subjective or objective based on their susceptibility to bias.
